questions.q: What are the three main ways money flows through our daily lives?
questions.a: The three ways are earning, spending, and saving. A wrong answer suggests the student hasn't grasped the basic cycle of personal finance and may be confusing "money" with just "wealth" or "coins."

questions.q: If a person spends every single rupee they earn each month, what problem might they face if they have a sudden medical emergency?
questions.a: They would have no savings to pay for the emergency, leading to financial distress. This shows the student understands the purpose of saving as a buffer for future uncertainty.

questions.q: A shopkeeper earns profit from sales, while a teacher earns a monthly salary. How are these two types of earnings similar?
questions.a: Both are forms of "earning" resulting from economic activity. A wrong answer suggests the student thinks only one type of work counts as "earning" money.

questions.q: Compare the difference between saving money for a bicycle (a specific goal) and saving money for an emergency (a general buffer).
questions.a: Saving for a bike is for a "want" or a planned purchase, while an emergency fund is for unpredictable events. A wrong answer shows the student does not distinguish between planned expenditure and contingency planning.

questions.q: Is it better to save money only after spending on all your wants? Why or why not?
questions.a: No, it is better to prioritize savings first, because if you wait until after spending on wants, you might have nothing left. This tests the student's ability to evaluate financial habits critically.

questions.q: Create a simple "budget" plan for a student who receives 100 rupees as pocket money for the week.
questions.a: A good plan allocates specific amounts for needs (e.g., pen), small wants (e.g., one chocolate), and a fixed portion for savings. A poor answer ignores saving entirely or spends more than the 100-rupee limit.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Money in daily life refers to the cycle of earning (gaining income through work), ______ (using money for goods and services), and saving (keeping money aside for future needs).
Fill in the blank: Think about the last time you ______ a pencil or a snack; where did that money come from, and why didn't you spend all your money at once?
What is Money in daily life? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Money in daily life refers to the cycle of earning (gaining income through work), spending (using money for goods and services), and saving (keeping money aside for future needs).

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Money in daily life?
questions.a: Students often believe that "saving" is only for rich people who have "extra" money.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to describe how their family earns, spends, and saves money, and explain why setting aside a portion of income is necessary for future security.
